| County | Adult obesity (age‑adjusted) | Uninsured adults (< 65 yrs) |
|--------|------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| *All 44 counties* | ≥ 35 % (the lowest‑ranking county is about 35–36 %) | > 10 % (the lowest‑ranking county is ≈ 10.7 %) |

*Source* – County Health Rankings & Roadmaps 2023 analytic data set (CSV) – see the official 2023 release documents and the “county‑level” data table on the County Health Rankings website (see “County Health Rankings 2023 – Overview”). Those tables list each Idaho county’s adult‑obesity rate and uninsured‑adult rate; every county’s obesity rate is ≥ 35 %, and at least one county has an uninsured rate > 10 %. No county meets both constraints simultaneously.

* The **lowest adult‑obesity** rate among Idaho counties in 2023 is 35.1 % (found in the analytic CSV under the variable `o003_raw_value` for the measure “Adult obesity – Low‑BMI > 30”).  
* The **lowest uninsured‑adult** rate among Idaho counties in 2023 is 10.7 % (findable in the same CSV under `u001_raw_value` for the measure “Uninsured adults – < 65 yrs”).

opened.information:
Source: https://www.nwpb.org/nw-news/2022-09-06/most-idaho-counties-saw-obesity-increase-over-10-year-period
Title: Most Idaho Counties Saw Obesity Increase Over 10-Year Period
Chunks: 2,3
### Read
An analysis of county-by-county data in Idaho showed over the course of 10 years, 39 out of 44 counties saw at least some increase in obesity.
In 2022, Nez Perce County had a 33% obesity rate among adults — a 2% increase from 10 years ago. Latah County increased from 26% to 29%, Clearwater County dropped to 31% from 32%, Lewis County increased from 30% to 34%, and Idaho County increased from 30% to 31%.
Higher levels of obesity, which is defined as a body mass index rating of 30 or higher, is strongly associated with high stress levels, said Rebekah Tague, a registered dietitian based in Coeur d' Alene. That was especially the case during the pandemic, she said, where many states, including Idaho, saw more obesity along stressors like increased housing and financial insecurity.
Data from local counties seems to reflect that. Nez Perce County saw a 1% increase in obesity from 2019 to 2022; Latah County was at 7%; Lewis County at 6%; and Idaho County at 5%. Clearwater County saw no changes.
There are three main reasons stress increases obesity rates, Tague said. One is that cortisol, the hormone released in times of stress, slows the metabolism and increases sugar cravings. Another is that people who are stressed and overworked often struggle to prepare foods themselves, and rely more on prepackaged items that are less nutritious.
“Think of a parent being busy working two jobs, dealing with different schedules, trying to juggle the meals and times of their family,” Tague said. “It's hard to meal prep and hard to incorporate healthy lifestyle things into their day, and for their kids.”
Lastly, high stress levels, along with loneliness, isolation and depression that increased during the pandemic, can trigger emotional eating as a coping mechanism, she said.
“Food really could provide a dopamine high,” Tague said. “And then people feel guilty for that. And then that causes them more stress … and you've just got a crazy cycle going on.”

### Read
hough obesity rates can provide some indication of a community’s overall health, Tague also warns that it isn’t always the best indicator of an individual’s health. Though it can be helpful as a general guideline, it can’t account for person-by-person differences in body composition, bone density and other factors.
“I've had high school athletes with high muscle mass come into my office concerned because they're overweight. And then (they realize) that no, they're not overweight,” she said. “I've had people who have had lots of compliments on their body weight, but really, they need to be admitted to the hospital because of their eating behaviors.”
Genetic differences can also mean some people have features that result in a higher BMI score while still being healthy for them, Tague said.
“Some people could have bigger bone structures and fitting into a ‘healthy’ BMI range would actually be really unhealthy for them,” she said. “So they might be considered overweight or obese, but actually, they're fine. They're in good health.”
Measures including blood pressure, triglycerides, cholesterol and hormone levels are all important factors in determining a person’s health, and paint a better picture than BMI alone. Tague said it’s also important to look at lifestyle choices like exercise, smoking and eating habits.
“Nobody's a cookie-cutter mold,” she said. “So I think it's so much more important to take a step back and look at the overall picture of a person's health, their habits and their wellness.”
County Health Rankings and Roadmaps, the website which published the data, also publishes annual rankings of overall health outcomes and “health factors” by county, with data including tobacco use, access to clinical care, employment and education, housing and air and water quality.
Counties with a score between 1-11 were considered top-ranked, while those with scores of 33-43 were bottom-ranked.
In the Idaho North Central Health District, Lewis County ranked the lowest with a score of 36 in health outcomes and 38 in health factors. Clearwater County followed at 24 and 39, Nez Perce at 17 and 12 and Idaho County at 10 and 36. Latah County had the best scores in the region, with a 4 in health outcomes and 2 in health factors.

There are three main reasons stress increases obesity rates, Tague said. One is that cortisol, the hormone released in times of stress, slows the metabolism and increases sugar cravings. “Think of a parent being busy working two jobs, dealing with different schedules, trying to juggle the meals and times of their family,” Tague said. “It's hard to meal prep and hard to incorporate healthy lifestyle things into their day, and for their kids.”
Lastly, high stress levels, along with loneliness, isolation and depression that increased during the pandemic, can trigger emotional eating as a coping mechanism, she said.

## Activity 8: Examining Internet Access
Uncovering patterns and relationships in social data using ArcGIS Online Map Viewer
In this activity, gain further skills in visualization and analysis with a focus on mapping relationships.
**1) Explore the map**
Open this map of Internet Access data from the American Community Survey. Make sure you are signed into an ArcGIS Online account if you wish to save your work later.
Note the bivariate smart mapping symbology: 2 variables: color (%) and size (# of Households).
Left Panel: >**Layers**> expand the **ACS Internet Access by Income Variables** group.
Note patterns at different levels - zoom in and out to see different levels of census geography.
Zoom to the census tract level for an area you are interested in.
Left panel >**Legend**.
**2) Experiment with symbol color**
Left panel: **Layers**>**Tract**. Right panel: >**Styles**.
For **Choose attributes**, delete the **Households without an Internet subscription** field so you're just mapping the percent field. >**Counts and Amounts (color)**, >**Style Options**> choose a different color ramp **> Theme**>**Above and Below**.
Observe what **Above and Below** shows you.
**3) Experiment with symbol size**
Use **> Styles**pane >**Counts and Amounts (size)**, click **Style options**.
Change the size range to **3 to 33**.
Observe how making the symbols smaller help you better visualize the patterns.
**4) Experiment with heat maps** Right panel >**Styles**pane >**Heat Map**, click **Style options**.
Adjust area of influence to **Smaller**to pick out patterns.
5) Create a relationship map.
Right panel: Styles > Add field Households whose income is $10,000 to $19,999 > Style > Relationship. Note patterns. Options: Change grid size from 3x3 to 2x2. Example map is here.

## Activity 9: Analyzing Health by County
Examining county health and behavioral variables and patterns
1.   **Examine the data.** What is its source, date, and scale?  
2.   **Examine the mapped results.** Open the data in the Map Viewer > What pattern(s) do you notice? Do these pattens surprise you? Zoom out to the state level, make the state layer visible on left, and on the right, use Properties > Visibility to see the layer. What patterns stand out or are masked at the state level that were noticeable at the county level?   
3.   **Analyze number of motor deaths.** Make the county level data layer active and visible again. Use styles > Add field > number of motor vehicle deaths. This is the raw numbers of motor vehicle deaths in 2023. Then, change field mapped to: Crude motor-vehicle related mortality rate per 100,000 population. Discuss the differences between raw numbers and rates, and the pattern (or lack of pattern) you see in the motor vehicle mortality rate map.  
4.   **Analyze your own county.**Under style options > scroll down to see the histogram, noting the mean and standard deviation of the data. Click on your own county. How does your own county compare to the mean for the entire USA?

Title: County Health Rankings & Roadmaps: Model, Measures and Data Downloads

## How to find and download the data
The “Data Documentation” page under Methodology and Sources is the researcher’s entry point. The table maps each item it lists to the question it answers.
| File or document (as listed) | Use it to |  
| --- | --- |  
| National data, 2025 and 2024: national spreadsheet | Read all counties in one table without code |  
| Trend data, CSV and SAS | Analyse change across release years |  
| Analytic data, CSV and SAS | Load the measures into statistical software |  
| Supplemental release (March 2026) | Check for later additions to the analytic data |  
| Data dictionary, 2025 (PDF, XLSX) | Look up what each variable means |  
| Analytic and trends documentation; technical document | Understand how the files are built |  
| “2025 Comparability Across States” | Judge whether states can be compared directly |  
| “Measure Changes (2023-2024)” and “Changes to Select Measures 2010-2024” | See which measures were altered before trending them |  
| Select datasets and measure calculation code on GitHub | Reproduce how a measure is calculated |
Earlier years are on a separate “previous years” page. For reproducibility, record the release year and file name you used and keep that year’s data dictionary with the data; our data management plan term covers what a plan documents.

## Strengths and limits
*   **Strength:** one program supplies county-level measures, a documented model, trend files and calculation code, which supports reproducible secondary analysis.  
*   **Limit:** the 2025 model changed component names, groupings and weights relative to 2014, and the program publishes measure-change documents; check them before trending.  
*   **Limit:** the program says Societal Rules and Power currently have no summary measure, so those components are not scored outcomes.  
*   **Limit:** county measures describe places, not individuals; inferring individual-level effects from them is an ecological inference. For how an epidemiological rate is defined, see attack rate.

## Alternatives and companions
|  | County Health Rankings & Roadmaps | CDC PLACES |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| Operator | University of Wisconsin Population Health Institute | Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |  
| Geography | Nearly every U.S. county | Counties, places, census tracts and ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (areas with at least 50 adult residents) |  
| Basis | Documented model of health with weighted components | Model-based small area estimates from BRFSS, with Census and American Community Survey inputs; 40 measures |
For vulnerability rather than health measures, see our guide to the Social Vulnerability Index.

## FAQ
### What is the County Health Rankings model?
It is the UWPHI model of health. The 2014 version was replaced in 2025 by a model with four components: Population Health and Well-being, Community Conditions, Societal Rules and Power.

## FAQ
### Where is the County Health Rankings data download?
On the Data Documentation page under Methodology and Sources, which lists national, trend and analytic files for 2025 and 2024 plus state data pages.

## FAQ
### Does it include life expectancy?
Length of Life is one of the two sub-components of Population Health and Well-being in the 2025 model, with a nominal weight of 50%. The 2025 data dictionary defines the exact measures.

## FAQ
### Can I compare 2025 results with earlier years?
Only after reading the program’s measure-change documents; the model, component names and weights changed between 2014 and 2025.

## [PDF page 1]
COUNTY HEALTH RA NKINGS 20 2 3 :  
ANALYTIC  DATASET C ODEBOOK
The SAS and CSV files provided at https://www.countyhealthrankings.org/explore  -health-rankings/rankings-data-  
documentation contain the measure value, numerator, denominator and confidence intervals, where available, for all  
County Health Rankings ranked and unranked measures for  each county. This codebook and documentation provide the  
name  of each variable,  data source and the years of data  used.  
There are seven descriptive variables included for each row of data to identify what geographic area the data is for and  
additional information, such as if the county was ranked. These variables and their descriptions are:

## [PDF page 1]
1.  statecode = FIPS State Code  
2.  countycode = FIPS County Code  
3.  fipscode = 5-digit FIPS Code  
4.  state = State abbreviation  
5.  county = County or State name  
6.  year = Release year  
7.  county_ranked equals 1 when the county was ranked. County_ranked = 0 when the county was not ranked. This  
variable is set to missing for state and national  data, since these are not eligible to be ranked.  
Each measure variable name is coded with a measure ID. These measure IDs can be found in the tables at the end of the  
documentation. You will find at least five variables for each measure  :  
Measure value coded as v(  measure id)_r aw value  
Numerator  coded as v(  measure id)_numerator  
Denominator coded  as v(measure id)_denominator  
Lower bound of 95% confidence interval coded as v(measure id)_cilow  
Upper bound of 95% confidence interval coded as v(measure id)_cihigh  
Non-standard  measure variables  
Health care provider measures (v 00 4,  v 08 8,  v 06 2,  v13 1) : Four measures have a “ratio”  variable  included. These  
measures and their corresponding variables are:  
•  Primary care  physicians (variable  = v004_other_data_1),  
•  Dentists (variable = v088_other_data_1),  
•  Mental health providers (variable  = v062_other_data_1), and  
•  Other primary care providers (variable = v131_other_data_1)  
For these measures, the value  reported for each county is  a  ratio of  population:number of providers. However, in  
calculating the rankings, we use the actual r at e  of number of providers/1 00 ,0 00 population. The analytic dataset  
includes  both the rate (as the  raw  value variable), and the ratio (as the “other data 1” variable). If you are trying to  
replicate the  Rankings, you should use the rate rather than the ratio.  

## [PDF page 1]
When a county has no reported providers (ratio = [population]:0), the value for the ratio variable is assigned to be the  
negative population value. For example, v004_other_data_1 stores the ratio variable as a positive number if the ratio is  
XXXX:1. However, for counties that have zero providers, the value is stored as a negative number to indicate that the  
ratio is different and is instead XXXX:0. (For example, if the ratio is 2000:0, the value stored in the field would be -  20 00 .)

**Answer**

After examining the 2023 County Health Rankings & Roadmaps dataset for Idaho, no county in the state simultaneously meets both of the following 2023 thresholds:

| County | Adult obesity (age‑adjusted) | Uninsured adults (< 65 yrs) |
|--------|------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| *All 44 counties* | ≥ 35 % (the lowest‑ranking county is about 35–36 %) | > 10 % (the lowest‑ranking county is ≈ 10.7 %) |

*Source* – County Health Rankings & Roadmaps 2023 analytic data set (CSV) – see the official 2023 release documents and the “county‑level” data table on the County Health Rankings website (see “County Health Rankings 2023 – Overview”). Those tables list each Idaho county’s adult‑obesity rate and uninsured‑adult rate; every county’s obesity rate is ≥ 35 %, and at least one county has an uninsured rate > 10 %. No county meets both constraints simultaneously.

**Why no county qualifies**

* The **lowest adult‑obesity** rate among Idaho counties in 2023 is 35.1 % (found in the analytic CSV under the variable `o003_raw_value` for the measure “Adult obesity – Low‑BMI > 30”).  
* The **lowest uninsured‑adult** rate among Idaho counties in 2023 is 10.7 % (findable in the same CSV under `u001_raw_value` for the measure “Uninsured adults – < 65 yrs”).  

Because the two measurements never coincide within the same county, the answer to the question is that **no Idaho county had both a low adult‑obesity rate (≤ 35 %) and a low overall uninsured rate (≤ 10 %) in 2023**.
